claims.text: In single-phase fcc multi-principal-element alloys, a three-dimensional hierarchical twin network governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness.
A hierarchical twin network both obstructs dislocation motion and provides pathways for dislocation glide.
The dual role of the twin network produces significant strain hardening without compromising ductility.
CrCoNi is a nominally equiatomic, single-phase fcc medium-entropy alloy.
CrCoNi has a very low or negative stacking-fault energy.
Deformation of CrCoNi can establish an extensive three-dimensional hierarchical twin network within individual grains.
Minor compositional additions can be selected that raise the stacking-fault energy of the baseline alloy.
Increasing stacking-fault energy will suppress deformation-twin formation.
Dynamic deformation at 600–800 °C promotes twin formation in the baseline alloy.
Twin barriers increase work hardening and strength.
Twin-boundary pathways permit substantial plastic deformation and thereby contribute to ductility and toughness.
The hierarchical twin network remains stable against detwinning as deformation continues.
The hierarchical twin network can form in grains approximately 5–50 μm in size.
Suppressing twinning by increasing stacking-fault energy will reduce strain hardening relative to the low-stacking-fault-energy baseline at 600–800 °C.
Suppressing twinning will reduce high-temperature plastic strain capacity and fracture toughness relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase fcc high- or medium-entropy alloys at 600–800 °C when grain size is about 5–50 μm and secondary phases are minimal.
Prior evidence supports deformation-twinning contributions at room and cryogenic temperatures, but its quantitative strengthening contribution remains uncertain.
The relative contributions of twinning, dynamic recovery, and nanoprecipitation at high temperature may depend on alloy chemistry and processing history.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome parenthetically equates toughness with plastic strain capacity before failure, whereas the experiment separately specifies fracture toughness such as KIc. Ductility/plastic strain capacity and fracture toughness are distinct outcomes, so the decisive endpoint is not defined consistently.
